name: Kepler Space Telescope
keyDiscovery: Revolutionized astronomy by discovering 2,662 confirmed exoplanets, proving statistically that planets outnumber stars in the Milky Way and that Earth-sized worlds in habitable zones are common throughout our galaxy.
missionLegacy: The foundational exoplanet mission that transformed astronomy from wondering if other solar systems existed to cataloging thousands of alien planetary architectures.
funFact: Kepler was so sensitive it could detect a flea crawling across a car headlight thousands of miles away! During its 9.6-year mission, it stared unblinkingly at over 530,000 stars.
heritageNote: Decommissioned on October 30, 2018 after completely exhausting its hydrazine fuel, Kepler now drifts in a safe, permanent heliocentric graveyard orbit trailing Earth.

objects.name: Kepler Space Observatory
objects.description: 0.95-meter Schmidt telescope with a 1.4-meter primary mirror and carbon-fiber sunshade. Weighs 1,052 kg and drifts in a perpetual Earth-trailing solar orbit.
objects.whySent: To determine the frequency of Earth-size planets in and near the habitable zones of Sun-like stars through high-precision transit photometry.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Proved that rocky super-Earths and sub-Neptunes are the most abundant class of planets in the galaxy, revolutionizing our understanding of planetary formation.
objects.ongoingScience: Kepler's archived transit light curves continue to reveal new exoplanets today through modern machine learning and automated vetting pipelines.
objects.firstPerson: I am the cosmic planet hunter! I am the Kepler Space Telescope. Before me, humanity had only spotted a few dozen weird giant gas planets. I stared at 150,000 stars at once for nearly a decade, watching for the tiniest dip in starlight as alien worlds crossed in front. I found 2,662 confirmed alien worlds! Now I drift peacefully in my graveyard solar orbit, knowing we are definitely not alone.

objects.name: 95-Megapixel CCD Focal Plane
objects.description: Focal plane array of 42 science CCDs covering a massive 115 square-degree field of view, measuring minute stellar brightness dips down to 20 parts per million.
objects.whySent: To achieve unprecedented photometric precision in space, capable of detecting the 0.0084% dimming of a Sun-like star when an Earth-size planet transits.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Discovered Kepler-186f and Kepler-452b, the first confirmed Earth-radius exoplanets orbiting in the habitable zones of their host stars.
objects.ongoingScience: CCD stellar calibration datasets remain the baseline standard for NASA's TESS and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
objects.firstPerson: The largest camera ever launched into space at the time! I am Kepler's 95-megapixel focal plane array. Curved like a bowl to match the telescope's optics, my 42 silicon chips counted millions of photons every six seconds. That micro-level precision discovered thousands of alien solar systems!

objects.name: Precision Reaction Wheel Assembly
objects.description: Set of four flywheels spun at thousands of RPM to impart gyroscopic torque for steady sub-arcsecond pointing without expending thruster propellant.
objects.source: NASA Ames K2 Mission Planning Guide / Howell et al.
objects.whySent: To hold the spacecraft absolutely motionless pointed at the Cygnus constellation for years at a time.
objects.scienceDiscovery: When two reaction wheels failed, engineers invented the 'K2 Mission', using solar radiation pressure balanced against the spacecraft body as a virtual third reaction wheel — extending the mission by four years!
objects.ongoingScience: Solar radiation pressure pointing algorithms developed for K2 are now standard contingency procedures for all deep-space space telescopes.
objects.firstPerson: Engineers called it the greatest hack in space history! When two of my spinning reaction wheels locked up, people thought Kepler was dead. But NASA engineers balanced the pressure of incoming sunlight particles against my solar panels like a rudder, turning solar wind into steering! We kept hunting planets for four more glorious years!

objects.name: Solar Array & Thermal Sunshade
objects.description: Curved carbon-composite sunshade and Gallium Arsenide solar array generating 1.1 kW of electrical power while thermally isolating the sensitive photometer at -85°C.
objects.whySent: To prevent blinding solar glare from entering the telescope aperture while keeping the optical assembly at cryogenic thermal equilibrium.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Proved that high-aspect carbon-composite baffle structures could maintain sub-millikelvin thermal stability in interplanetary space.
objects.ongoingScience: Baffle designs directly influenced the sunshield geometry of the James Webb Space Telescope and Roman Space Telescope.
objects.firstPerson: Keeping things frosty in direct sunlight! I am the Kepler sunshield. I shielded the ultra-sensitive optical detector from the Sun's blazing heat while collecting 1,100 watts of solar juice from my curved panels. Without me, the starlight sensors would have been blinded on day one!
